set.st: Cornelius and Stephen Horrigan distrusted banks and were said to have hidden money around their farm, which the AP put about 17 miles from Boscobel. On 11 Nov 1930 three men posing as hunters, with a well-dressed woman, came to the farm. They had asked earlier for permission to hunt on it. They killed Patrick Gorman, 65, and his son Paul, 18, visitors from Huron, South Dakota, and wounded both brothers (Stephen was shot through the arm and Cornelius's jaw was shattered), but fled without searching. Their sister Ellen, 75, kept house. The case was worked from Prairie du Chien, and a suspect was arrested at a Wauzeka roadhouse. Neighbors said there were many stories of buried treasure on the homestead, and many people had dug over the farm. The summer before, three men and a woman had been run off it while digging. The Soldiers Grove paper also says three men were fought off in another attempt about six weeks before the murders. Two local papers place the farm: the Grant County Herald (12 Nov 1930) says 'the Horrigan farm near Mt. Zion', and the Muscoda Leader-Press (27 Nov 1930) says 'between Mt. Zion and Soldiers Grove'. GNIS has Horrigan Ridge about 5 km NE of Mt. Zion, about 12 miles in a straight line from Boscobel. The Herald names the brothers as William and Cornelius, while the AP has Stephen. Pin: Horrigan Ridge (GNIS 1566706), sec. 35 T10N R3W, Crawford County, between Mt. Zion and Soldiers Grove. The exact farmstead needs a 1920s-30s Crawford plat. The 1914 Crawford County atlas spells the name Horgen and shows the brothers' land, about 760 acres, in secs. 25, 26, 35 and 36 of Clayton township. The papers gave 630 acres. The pin is now on the building by the road junction on C. M. Horgen's land. Placed: the c.1915 county plat shows Horrigan land across the north tier of sec. 2, Town of Scott, Crawford County, 16.7 miles due north of Boscobel, which fits '17 miles from Boscobel'. Private farm: ask permission. Local paper: the brothers distrusted banks and buried their money on the farm; robbers tried at least three times (the 1922 holdup, put at c.1923 in the Scout, took anywhere from a few hundred to $40,000 by differing reports; the 1930 attempt ended in murder); diggers worked the ground in all directions around the house. No find reported 1931-45. Private: permission. The Dial's account of the 11 Nov 1930 bandit raid on the Horrigan farm, in which two brothers were shot, names the suspects held in Chicago but says nothing of money hidden or found. The Muscoda Leader-Press of 13 Nov 1930 put the farm home '4 miles west of Tavera' and said the brothers had twice before defended the place against marauders drawn by reports of thousands of dollars in gold buried about the premises; they did not trust banks and had 'secreted their wealth in caches on the farm'. The 1922 papers fix the first holdup at 24 July 1922: about $40,000 taken from a trunk, $5,000 of it in gold, and the Dial already notes the family's habit of hiding money about the farm. Nothing from that robbery was reported recovered.

set.st: Several versions of one legend. Soldiers from Fort Crawford crossing to McGregor's landing with $8,000 in gold to pay the Fort Atkinson garrison were killed by Indians after burying it on a hill, said to be the Heights; other tellings have a canoe of gold sunk in the Mississippi, a sack buried near Fort Crawford, or $80,000 buried by four of Col. Zachary Taylor's soldiers near North McGregor. A Decorah paper's 1905 version put the sum at $890,000 [sic; probably $80,000] in four bags of soldiers' pay from Colonel Taylor's stockade in 1830, hidden from the Indians by four men and 'never found about the bluff'. Early settlers hunted the hills, and in 1913 a man with a 'gold magnet' came to McGregor to search. In 1937 a girl found an 1851 $10 gold piece on a Mississippi river hill south of McGregor; years earlier three children had found a $20 gold piece on the same side hill a little to the north, and the paper suggested both had washed down from a cache higher in the bluff. A farm west of McGregor was nicknamed the 'Gold Mine' farm for all the digging there. Pin is approximate, not the spot itself. The 1905 wire as printed: in 1830 four bags of gold coin, $80,000 for the soldiers' pay, reached Col. Zachary Taylor's fort ('Fort McKay'). Fearing attack, he sent four trusted men to hide them; the fort was attacked, and after days of fighting the four were found dead. A scrap of paper near the body of the man called Mercierre said the money was 'buried on the highest of the bluffs across from the place where they were found'. Parties searched and found nothing; 'hundreds of people have worked by the day' on the lonely bluff near North McGregor, and in 1905 a premium was being offered. The 1906 syndicate feature printed the note as 'ON HIGHEST BLUFF ACROSS FROM FORT IN 4 PILES EACH 20,000 PIERRE MERCIERRE' and put Fort McKay 'near where the little town of North McGregor, Iowa, now stands'. In Feb 1905 hundreds were digging on the bluff, and Taylor's parties dug for days in 1906; 'never a trace was found'.
